newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian reporters seized, imam killed in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russian reporters seized, imam killed in Chechnya.

text.p: Two Russian journalists were kidnapped in broad daylight on Wednesday in the centre of the Chechen capital Grozny, Russian news agencies reported.
Itar-Tass news agency said the journalists worked for the Vzglyad (View) programme, produced by the independent VID production company.
The company and Chechen officials declined comment.

Tass said the journalists, a reporter and a cameraman, had been seized by masked men at around 2 p.m. (1000 GMT). They were waiting by their car when two other vehicles arrived with the kidnappers who fired into the air and then made off with their hostages.
Vzglyad, a weekly current affairs programme on the ORT channel, recently aired an interview with a Chechen who said he belonged to a gang trying to make money from kidnapping journalists.
Tass said the kidnapped journalist had conducted the interview with the Chechen hostage-taker.
Officials deny they have paid ransoms to secure the release of those freed earlier.

Kidnapping and other crimes are common in rebel Chechnya, where most men are still armed after the region's 21-month war with Russian troops and where jobs are scarce in a region wrecked by the conflict.
Tens of thousands of people died in the fighting which ended last August.
Last Friday, four Russian journalists were released after three months of captivity in Chechnya.
A television crew of three from NTV commercial television is still being held, though Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov is personally heading efforts to free them.

Dozens, if not hundreds, of people of other professions are still missing in Chechnya, but the Russia media have give a much higher profile to their kidnapped colleagues. The kidnapping, likely to marr the relations between Moscow and the separatist region which have markedly improved recently, followed the killing of the cleric of an important mosque in Grozny on Tuesday.

The imam's family said the unidentified gunman, who burst into their home on Tuesday, was a member of the strict Wahabi sect. He shouted abuse about the imam's sermons before shooting Khasanbek Yakhyayev, who was in his 70s, with a Kalashnikov assault rifle.
Relatives of the imam caught up with the gunman as he walked away and dragged him back to the house, where they shot him in front of witnesses next to the body of his victim.
Tass quoted Chechen Interior Minister Kazbek Makhashev as denying the murder was religiously motivated. He said it was the result of a spontaneous quarrel.
There has been tension between Wahabis and the Moslem majority in various parts of southern Russia.

At least two people died in a gun battle last month involving about 1,000 people in neighbouring Dagestan. The Wahabi sect follows the official doctrine of Saudi Arabia's reigning house and favours traditional Islamic values.

Blood feuds continue in several southern Russian areas despite efforts by former Soviet leaders to stamp them out. On Tuesday, the leader of Ingushetia, neighbouring Chechnya, proposed legalising the tradition.
In Chechnya, elements of Islamic law or sharia, introduced by the separatist leadership, are supposed to prevent people taking the law into their own hands.
